questions.stem:
Consider the function $f(x) = -2(x - 1)(x + 3)$, for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. The following diagram shows part of the graph of $f$.

![A downward parabola crossing the x-axis on both sides of the y-axis, with its vertex to the left of the y-axis.](content/papers/img/2021-nov-p1-q1.png)

parts.label: a
parts.markscheme:
(i) setting $f(x) = 0$ ***(M1)***

$x = 1$, $x = -3$ (accept $(1,\ 0)$, $(-3,\ 0)$) ***A1***

(ii) **METHOD 1**

$x = -1$ ***A1***

substituting their $x$-coordinate into $f$ ***(M1)***

$y = 8$ ***A1***

$(-1,\ 8)$

**METHOD 2**

attempt to complete the square ***(M1)***

$-2\left((x + 1)^2 - 4\right)$

$x = -1$, $y = 8$ ***A1A1***

$(-1,\ 8)$

parts.label: b
parts.intro: The function $f$ can be written in the form $f(x) = -2(x - h)^2 + k$.
parts.text: Write down the value of $h$ and the value of $k$.

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 4}{3 - x}$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 3$.

parts.label: a
b
c
parts.text:
Sketch the graph of $f$ on the axes below.

![Empty axes with x and y from −15 to 15.](content/papers/img/2021-nov-p1-q3-axes.png)
parts.markscheme:
![Graph of f: two branches with vertical asymptote x = 3 and horizontal asymptote y = −2.](content/papers/img/2021-nov-p1-q3c-ms.png)

***A1***

> **Note:** Award ***A1*** for completely correct shape: two branches in correct quadrants with asymptotic behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.markscheme:
**METHOD 1**

attempt to write all LHS terms with a common denominator of $x - 1$ ***(M1)***

$2x - 3 - \dfrac{6}{x - 1} = \dfrac{2x(x - 1) - 3(x - 1) - 6}{x - 1}$ OR $\dfrac{(2x - 3)(x - 1)}{x - 1} - \dfrac{6}{x - 1}$

$= \dfrac{2x^2 - 2x - 3x + 3 - 6}{x - 1}$ OR $\dfrac{2x^2 - 5x + 3}{x - 1} - \dfrac{6}{x - 1}$ ***A1***

$= \dfrac{2x^2 - 5x - 3}{x - 1}$ ***AG***

**METHOD 2**

attempt to use algebraic division on RHS ***(M1)***

correctly obtains quotient of $2x - 3$ and remainder $-6$ ***A1***

$= 2x - 3 - \dfrac{6}{x - 1}$ as required. ***AG***

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence or otherwise, solve the equation $2\sin 2\theta - 3 - \dfrac{6}{\sin 2\theta - 1} = 0$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$, $\theta \neq \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
parts.markscheme:
consider the equation $\dfrac{2\sin^2 2\theta - 5\sin 2\theta - 3}{\sin 2\theta - 1} = 0$ ***(M1)***

$\Rightarrow 2\sin^2 2\theta - 5\sin 2\theta - 3 = 0$

**EITHER**

attempt to factorise in the form $(2\sin 2\theta + a)(\sin 2\theta + b)$ ***(M1)***

> **Note:** Accept any variable in place of $\sin 2\theta$.

$(2\sin 2\theta + 1)(\sin 2\theta - 3) = 0$

**OR**

attempt to substitute into quadratic formula ***(M1)***

$\sin 2\theta = \dfrac{5 \pm \sqrt{49}}{4}$

**THEN**

$\sin 2\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin 2\theta = 3$ ***(A1)***

> **Note:** Award ***A1*** for $\sin 2\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ only.

one of $\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ OR $\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ (accept $210$ or $330$) ***(A1)***

$\theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12}$ (must be in radians) ***A1***

> **Note:** Award ***A0*** if additional answers given.

questions.stem:
Consider a function $f$ with domain $a < x < b$. The following diagram shows the graph of $f'$, the derivative of $f$.

![Graph of f′ for a < x < b: it crosses the x-axis at p, has a local maximum at q, passes through the origin, has a local minimum at r and touches the x-axis at a local maximum at t.](content/papers/img/2021-nov-p1-q9.png)

The graph of $f'$, the derivative of $f$, has $x$-intercepts at $x = p$, $x = 0$ and $x = t$. There are local maximum points at $x = q$ and $x = t$ and a local minimum point at $x = r$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find all the values of $x$ where the graph of $f$ is increasing. Justify your answer.
parts.markscheme:
> **Special note:** In this question if candidates use the word ‘gradient’ in their reasoning. e.g. gradient is positive, it must be clear whether this is the gradient of $f$ or the gradient of $f'$ to earn the ***R*** mark.

$f$ increases when $p < x < 0$ ***A1***

$f$ increases when $f'(x) > 0$ OR $f'$ is above the $x$-axis ***R1***

> **Note:** Do not award ***A0R1***.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of $x$ where the graph of $f$ has a local maximum.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(i) Find the value of $x$ where the graph of $f$ has a local minimum. Justify your answer.

(ii) Find the values of $x$ where the graph of $f$ has points of inflexion. Justify your answer.
parts.markscheme:
(i) $f$ is minimum when $x = p$ ***A1***

because $f'(p) = 0$, $f'(x) < 0$ when $x < p$ and $f'(x) > 0$ when $x > p$ (may be seen in a sign diagram clearly labelled as $f'$)

OR because $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $x = p$

OR $f'(p) = 0$ and slope of $f'$ is positive at $x = p$ ***R1***

> **Note:** Do not award ***A0 R1***.

(ii) $f$ has points of inflexion when $x = q$, $x = r$ and $x = t$ ***A2***

$f'$ has turning points at $x = q$, $x = r$ and $x = t$

OR

$f''(q) = 0$, $f''(r) = 0$ and $f''(t) = 0$ and $f'$ changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa at each of these $x$-values (may be seen in a sign diagram clearly labelled as $f''$ and $f'$) ***R1***

> **Note:** Award ***A0*** if any incorrect answers are given. Do not award ***A0R1***.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
The total area of the region enclosed by the graph of $f'$, the derivative of $f$, and the $x$-axis is $20$.

Given that $f(p) + f(t) = 4$, find the value of $f(0)$.
parts.markscheme:
recognizing area from $p$ to $t$ (seen anywhere) ***M1***

$\displaystyle\int_p^t \lvert f'(x)\rvert\,\mathrm{d}x$

recognizing to negate integral for area below $x$-axis ***(M1)***

$\displaystyle\int_p^0 f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^t f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ OR $\displaystyle\int_p^0 f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_t^0 f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

$\displaystyle\int_m^n f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = f(n) - f(m)$ (for any integral) ***(M1)***

$f(0) - f(p) - [f(t) - f(0)]$ OR $f(0) - f(p) + f(0) - f(t)$ ***(A1)***

$2f(0) - [f(t) + f(p)] = 20$, $2f(0) - 4 = 20$ ***(A1)***

$f(0) = 12$ ***A1***
